questions.stem: In VCE Legal Studies, social cohesion is best described as a state in which:
options: members of society work together and feel safe and a sense of belonging
every member of society holds the same political and moral values
laws are enforced only when most of the community agrees with them
courts settle every dispute before it can reach the parliament
questions.explanation: Social cohesion describes a society whose members cooperate, feel safe and belong, even though they hold different views. It does not require everyone to share the same values; laws and the legal system exist partly to manage those differences peacefully.

questions.stem: Which action by an individual best helps to achieve social cohesion?
options: Refusing to serve on a jury after receiving a summons
Reporting a crime they witnessed to Victoria Police
Ignoring a local council by-law they consider unfair
Removing a neighbour's fence to settle a boundary dispute
questions.explanation: Individuals support social cohesion by obeying laws and helping the legal system enforce them, for example by reporting crime. Ignoring a by-law, taking matters into one's own hands or refusing jury service all weaken the system that keeps society orderly.

questions.stem: The legal system helps to achieve social cohesion mainly by:
options: ensuring that no disputes ever arise between members of society
allowing victims of crime to punish wrongdoers themselves
making only laws that every adult citizen has voted to approve
providing peaceful ways to resolve disputes and enforce laws
questions.explanation: Disputes are inevitable, so the legal system's role is to resolve them peacefully through courts, tribunals and other bodies, and to enforce laws. Allowing people to punish wrongdoers themselves would undermine order rather than support it.

questions.stem: A Victorian law requires employers to provide a safe workplace. This law mainly protects:
options: the right of employers to set their own safety standards
the right of workers to choose their own wage rates
the right of the public to inspect any workplace at will
the right of workers to be free from harm at work
questions.explanation: Workplace safety laws protect workers' right to be safe at work by placing duties on employers. They limit, rather than protect, an employer's freedom to set its own standards.

questions.stem: A council by-law bans amplified music in a park after 10 pm. Which statement best explains how this law balances rights?
options: It removes all rights from park users so that nearby residents can enjoy absolute rights instead
It cannot balance rights at all, because by-laws are made by councils rather than by parliament
It restricts park users' freedom to play music to protect nearby residents' quiet enjoyment of their homes
It protects the rights of park users only, because it applies just after 10 pm each night
questions.explanation: Many laws limit one person's freedom to protect another's rights; here, a limited restriction on noise protects residents at night. A by-law is delegated legislation made under the authority of an Act, so it is a law with legal force even though a council made it.

questions.stem: In VCE Legal Studies, the principle of fairness means that:
options: all people who break the same law receive exactly the same sanction from the courts
all people can participate in the justice system and its processes are impartial and open
all people engaging with the justice system and its processes are treated in the same way
all people can engage with the justice system and its processes on an informed basis
questions.explanation: Fairness is about participation and impartial, open processes. Being treated in the same way is the principle of equality, and engaging on an informed basis is the principle of access.

questions.stem: As defined in VCE Legal Studies, the principle of equality includes the idea that:
options: if the same treatment creates disadvantage, adequate measures should be taken to remove it
the processes of the justice system should be impartial and open to the public
people should understand their legal rights and know how to enforce them
every accused person must receive a lawyer paid for by Victoria Legal Aid
questions.explanation: Equality means people are treated in the same way, and where identical treatment creates disparity, measures should allow everyone to engage without disadvantage. Impartial and open processes belong to fairness, and understanding one's rights belongs to access.

questions.stem: Which principle of justice is concerned with people being able to engage with the justice system on an informed basis?
options: Fairness
Equality
Precedent
Access
questions.explanation: Access means all people should be able to engage with the justice system and its processes on an informed basis. Fairness concerns participation and impartial, open processes, while precedent is a method of court law-making, not a principle of justice.

questions.stem: Members of the public may sit in the public gallery during most criminal trials in Victoria. This most directly upholds which principle of justice?
options: Precedent, because courts follow past cases
Fairness, because the process is open
Equality, because everyone is treated alike
Access, because people are informed of the law
questions.explanation: Open courts allow the public to see that justice is done, which reflects fairness: processes should be impartial and open. Equality is about the same treatment of the people engaging with the system, not public scrutiny of the process.

questions.stem: Victoria Legal Aid publishes free, plain-language guides explaining what happens at a person's first court hearing. This mainly promotes the principle of:
options: equality
deterrence
access
fairness
questions.explanation: Plain-language guides help people engage with the justice system on an informed basis, which is the principle of access. Deterrence is a purpose of sanctions, not a principle of justice.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the principle of equality from the principle of fairness?
options: Equality is about people being treated in the same way; fairness is about participation and impartial, open processes
Equality is about participation and impartial, open processes; fairness is about people being treated in the same way
Equality applies only in criminal cases; fairness applies only in civil disputes heard in courts and tribunals
Equality is about knowing one's legal rights; fairness is about the cost of obtaining legal representation
questions.explanation: The study design defines equality as the same treatment for all (with measures where that treatment creates disadvantage) and fairness as participation and impartial, open processes. Students often swap the two, and both principles apply across the criminal and civil justice systems.

questions.stem: A law written in plain language that ordinary people can follow most clearly shows which characteristic of an effective law?
options: It is enforceable
It reflects society's values
It is clear and understood
It is stable
questions.explanation: An effective law should be clear and understood, so that people know exactly what is required of them. Stability is about the law not changing too often, which is a separate characteristic.

questions.stem: A law bans using a mobile phone inside your own home after midnight. Police have no practical way to detect breaches. Which characteristic of an effective law does it most clearly lack?
options: It is not known
It is not clear and understood
It is not enforceable
It is not stable
questions.explanation: A law that cannot practically be policed or proven is not enforceable, so people may ignore it without consequence. Nothing in the scenario suggests the law changes often, is unpublished or is unclear.

questions.stem: Parliament amends a road law several times in one year, each time changing what drivers must do. Which characteristic of an effective law is most at risk?
options: Reflecting society's values
Clarity of wording
Stability
Enforceability
questions.explanation: An effective law should be stable, so that people can rely on it and plan their behaviour. Frequent changes undermine that certainty even if each version is clearly worded and enforceable.

questions.stem: Laws against cruelty to animals have been strengthened over time as community attitudes changed. This shows that an effective law should:
options: be enforceable
be clear and understood by all
reflect society's values
be stable
questions.explanation: Laws are changed so they keep reflecting society's values, and stronger animal protection laws followed changing community attitudes. Stability is a separate characteristic and is in some tension with change.

questions.stem: Before a new road rule begins, the government runs a public awareness campaign on television and online. This mainly helps the law to be:
options: known
stable
enforceable
consistent with precedent
questions.explanation: People can only obey a law they know about, so publicising it helps the law be known. A campaign does not make a law any easier to police or any less likely to change.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains a tension between two characteristics of an effective law?
options: A law should reflect changing values, but changing it too often undermines its stability
A law should be known, but publishing it widely makes it harder for police to enforce
A law should be clear, but a clearly worded law cannot reflect society's values
A law should be enforceable, but a law that is enforced can no longer be stable
questions.explanation: Reflecting society's values sometimes requires change, while stability requires the law not to change too often, so law-makers must balance the two. Publishing a law does not make it harder to enforce, and clear wording is compatible with reflecting values.

questions.stem: The main law-making role of the Victorian Parliament is to:
options: create common law through precedent
interpret Acts when disputes arise in court
make, amend and repeal statute law
decide criminal trials where the accused pleads not guilty
questions.explanation: Parliament is the supreme law-maker: it makes new statutes and can amend or repeal existing ones. Creating common law and interpreting Acts are the courts' law-making roles, and juries and judges, not parliament, decide trials.

questions.stem: Courts make law mainly through:
options: the doctrine of precedent and statutory interpretation
passing bills through both houses of parliament
making regulations under the authority of an Act of parliament
holding referendums on proposed changes to the law
questions.explanation: When courts decide cases they create precedents and interpret the meaning of statutes, both of which make law. Regulations are delegated legislation made by subordinate bodies, and bills are passed by parliament, not courts.

questions.stem: The Supreme Court of Victoria creates a new common law rule. The Victorian Parliament disagrees with the rule. Parliament may:
options: ask the Governor to dismiss the judges for the decision
pass a statute that overrides the common law rule
order the Supreme Court to rehear the case
lodge an appeal against the decision in the Court of Appeal
questions.explanation: Parliament is supreme over the courts in law-making, so a statute can abrogate (override) a common law rule. Parliament is not a party to the case and cannot appeal, and judges cannot be removed simply because parliament disagrees with their decisions.

questions.stem: Courts must sometimes interpret the words of an Act because:
options: every Act expires after ten years unless a court confirms it again
judges are elected to review the wording of each new bill before it passes
the words may be ambiguous or may not cover a situation parliament did not foresee
an Act cannot come into force until a court has approved its wording
questions.explanation: Statutes are written in general terms, so courts must decide what words mean when they are unclear or when new situations arise. Courts do not approve, confirm or review bills before they become law; that is parliament's process.

questions.stem: Parliament passes an Act that puts into statute form a set of rules first developed by the courts. This is known as:
options: codification
abrogation
statutory interpretation
distinguishing
questions.explanation: Codifying common law means enacting judge-made rules as statute, often with refinements. Abrogation is the opposite relationship, where a statute overrides or abolishes a common law rule.

questions.stem: A court interprets the word 'vehicle' in an Act to include an electric scooter. Later, parliament amends the Act to exclude electric scooters. What is the effect?
options: The interpretation still binds lower courts, as precedent outranks statute
The amendment is invalid because a court has already ruled on the issue
The amendment has no effect until the Court of Appeal confirms it
The amendment overrides the court's interpretation for future cases
questions.explanation: Because parliament is supreme in law-making, it can respond to a court's interpretation by amending the statute, and courts must then apply the new wording. Precedent never outranks a valid statute, and parliament does not need court approval to amend its own Acts.

questions.stem: The part of a judgment that forms a binding precedent for lower courts is the:
options: statement of compatibility
ratio decidendi
obiter dictum
dissenting judgment
questions.explanation: The ratio decidendi is the legal reasoning essential to the decision, and it binds lower courts in the same hierarchy. Obiter dicta are remarks 'by the way' and are only persuasive.

questions.stem: A County Court judge is bound to follow the ratio decidendi of a decision made by the:
options: Magistrates' Court of Victoria
Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of New South Wales
County Court, in an earlier case before another judge
Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Victoria
questions.explanation: Precedents bind courts lower in the same hierarchy, and the Court of Appeal sits above the County Court in Victoria. Decisions of courts in other states are persuasive only, and decisions of lower courts or courts of the same level do not bind.

questions.stem: A Supreme Court of Victoria judge is considering a decision of the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom on the same legal issue. That decision is:
options: binding, because Australian law developed from English common law
irrelevant, because courts cannot consider decisions from other countries
persuasive, so the judge may consider it but is not bound to follow it
binding, because it comes from a final court of appeal
questions.explanation: Decisions of overseas courts can be persuasive in Victoria but are never binding. Although Australian common law developed from English law, English decisions have not bound Australian courts for decades.

questions.stem: A judge decides that the material facts of a case are different enough from an earlier binding case that the precedent does not need to be followed. This is called:
options: overruling
reversing on appeal
disapproving
distinguishing
questions.explanation: Distinguishing allows a court to avoid a binding precedent because the material facts differ. Overruling is when a higher court in a later case decides an earlier precedent was wrong.

questions.stem: The Court of Appeal hears an appeal in the same case and overturns the County Court's decision. This is called:
options: reversing
overruling
distinguishing
disapproving
questions.explanation: Reversing happens in the same case on appeal, when a higher court changes the lower court's decision. Overruling happens in a later, different case, when a higher court decides an earlier precedent is no longer good law.

questions.stem: The rule that a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the consumer of its product was first set out by judges deciding a case. This rule is best classified as:
options: statute law and civil law
common law and criminal law
statute law and criminal law
common law and civil law
questions.explanation: A rule made by judges in deciding a case is common law, and a duty of care between private parties is part of civil law (the tort of negligence). It would be statute law only if parliament had enacted it.

questions.stem: Section 72 of the Crimes Act 1958 (Vic), which defines the offence of theft, is best classified as:
options: common law and civil law
statute law and criminal law
common law and criminal law
statute law and civil law
questions.explanation: The Crimes Act 1958 is an Act of the Victorian Parliament, so it is statute law, and theft is an offence against society, so it is criminal law. A source of law is about who made it, and a type of law is about what it governs.

questions.stem: Regulations made by a government department under the authority of an Act of parliament are known as:
options: judge-made common law
obiter dicta
codified precedent
delegated legislation
questions.explanation: Parliament can delegate law-making power to subordinate bodies such as departments and councils, which make regulations and by-laws. Common law is made by judges in decided cases.

questions.stem: Which court is at the top of the Victorian court hierarchy?
options: The Magistrates' Court
The Children's Court
The Supreme Court (Court of Appeal)
The County Court
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court, through its Court of Appeal, is the highest court in Victoria. Appeals from it go to the High Court of Australia, which is a federal court and not part of the Victorian hierarchy.

questions.stem: Which court is the final court of appeal for Victorian cases?
options: The High Court of Australia
The Supreme Court of Victoria
The Federal Court of Australia
The County Court of Victoria
questions.explanation: The High Court of Australia hears appeals from all state and territory courts and is the final court of appeal in Australia. The Federal Court deals with federal matters and does not hear appeals from the Victorian Court of Appeal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a reason for having a court hierarchy?
options: It allows parliament to review and change court decisions
It means every case can be heard by a jury
It ensures that all cases begin in the Supreme Court
It allows parties to appeal a decision to a higher court
questions.explanation: The four reasons for a court hierarchy are appeals, specialisation, administrative convenience and the doctrine of precedent. Most cases begin in the Magistrates' Court, and parliament does not review court decisions.

questions.stem: Minor cases are heard in the Magistrates' Court so that serious cases can go to higher courts with more experienced judges and more resources. This reflects which reason for the court hierarchy?
options: Administrative convenience
Appeals
The doctrine of precedent
The separation of powers
questions.explanation: Administrative convenience means cases are allocated to courts by their seriousness and complexity, so resources are used efficiently. Appeals concern a party asking a higher court to review a decision, which is not what the scenario describes.

questions.stem: Victoria has a Coroners Court that investigates deaths and a Children's Court that deals with matters involving young people. This mainly reflects which reason for a court hierarchy?
options: Appeals
The doctrine of precedent
The rule of law
Specialisation
questions.explanation: Specialised courts develop expertise in particular kinds of matters, such as coronial inquests or cases involving children. The doctrine of precedent is about lower courts following higher courts' decisions, not about developing expertise.

questions.stem: Lower courts must follow the legal reasoning of higher courts in the same hierarchy. Which reason for the court hierarchy does this describe?
options: Appeals
Specialisation
Administrative convenience
The doctrine of precedent
questions.explanation: The doctrine of precedent depends on a hierarchy, because a binding precedent must come from a higher court in the same hierarchy. Specialisation concerns courts developing expertise, not following decisions.

questions.stem: Mia is convicted in the County Court. She believes the judge gave the jury an incorrect direction about the law. The court hierarchy allows her to:
options: appeal to the Magistrates' Court for a rehearing
ask the same jury to reconsider its verdict later
appeal directly to the Victorian Parliament
seek leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal
questions.explanation: The hierarchy allows a person to have a decision reviewed by a higher court, and appeals from County Court trials go to the Court of Appeal, usually with leave. The Magistrates' Court is lower in the hierarchy, and parliament does not hear appeals.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes criminal law?
options: Laws that are made only by judges in decided cases
Laws that apply only to the actions of government departments
Laws that define offences against society and set out sanctions
Laws that govern disputes between individuals and allow remedies
questions.explanation: Criminal law defines behaviour that is an offence against society and sets out the sanctions for it. Laws governing private disputes and remedies are civil law, and criminal law can come from statute or common law.

questions.stem: In a criminal case, the parties are known as:
options: the plaintiff and the accused
the applicant and the respondent
the prosecution and the accused
the plaintiff and the defendant
questions.explanation: The state brings a criminal case through the prosecution against the accused. The plaintiff and defendant are the parties in a civil case, and applicant and respondent are terms used in tribunals and some applications.

questions.stem: Which correctly matches each type of law with its standard of proof?
options: Criminal: beyond reasonable doubt; civil: on the balance of probabilities
Criminal: on the balance of probabilities; civil: beyond reasonable doubt
Criminal: beyond reasonable doubt; civil: beyond reasonable doubt
Criminal: beyond all possible doubt; civil: on the balance of probabilities
questions.explanation: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, while a plaintiff must prove their case on the balance of probabilities. The criminal standard is high but does not require proof beyond all possible doubt.

questions.stem: Sam punches Leo outside a nightclub, breaking his jaw. Which statement is correct?
options: Leo can sue Sam in a civil action only if the criminal prosecution fails
Sam may be prosecuted for a criminal offence and also sued by Leo in a civil action
Sam can be prosecuted or sued for the punch, but the law does not allow both
Leo must choose whether the state prosecutes Sam or whether he sues Sam himself
questions.explanation: One act can breach both criminal law and civil law, so the state may prosecute Sam for assault and Leo may sue him for compensation. The two cases are separate and neither depends on the other's outcome.

questions.stem: Sam is acquitted at his criminal trial for assaulting Leo. Leo then sues Sam for the same incident. Which statement is correct?
options: Leo cannot win, because a civil case must follow the verdict of a criminal trial
Leo may win only if new evidence emerges that was not used at the criminal trial
Leo may still win, because the civil standard of proof is lower than the criminal standard
Leo cannot win, because the acquittal proves Sam did not cause the injury
questions.explanation: An acquittal means guilt was not proven beyond reasonable doubt, not that the accused is innocent. Leo needs only to prove his case on the balance of probabilities, so he may succeed on the same evidence.

questions.stem: The main aim of a civil action is usually to:
options: punish the defendant on behalf of the whole community
deter other members of the community from committing similar crimes in future
protect society by removing the defendant from the community
restore the plaintiff, as far as possible, to their position before the wrong
questions.explanation: Civil law gives a wronged party a remedy, usually damages that aim to put them back in the position they were in before the breach. Punishing, deterring and protecting society are purposes of criminal sanctions.
